QF.id: Clubbing, Set-Off and Carry Forward of Losses_18

question.text: Mrs. Lata gifted Rs.5,00,000 to her minor daughter (age 10, no disability) who earned Rs.35,000 as interest income. Lata's total income is Rs.12,00,000 and her husband's income is Rs.8,00,000. What amount is added to Lata's total income due to clubbing?

answer.text: Rs.35,000 — full amount clubbed with the higher-earning parent
Rs.33,500 — clubbed with husband as he is the father, with Rs.1,500 exemption
Rs.33,500 — clubbed with Lata (higher income parent) after Rs.1,500 per child exemption
Nil — income from gifts by parents is not clubbed

explanation.text: The Logic: Section 64(1A) of the Income Tax Act clubs a minor child's income with the parent whose total income — before this clubbing — is higher. Lata earns Rs.12,00,000 and her husband Rs.8,00,000, so the minor daughter's Rs.35,000 interest income is clubbed with Lata, not with the father. Section 10(32) then allows a Rs.1,500 per-child-per-year exemption from the clubbed income. Amount added to Lata's total income = Rs.35,000 - Rs.1,500 = Rs.33,500. The disability exception does not apply (no disability) and there is no manual-work / skill-talent income to exclude. The Trap: Option A applies clubbing but forgets the Section 10(32) Rs.1,500 exemption. Option B applies the exemption correctly but clubs with the father by default — the rule is gender-neutral and follows income, not parental role. Option D incorrectly treats gifts from a parent as outside the clubbing net, but the issue is income from the gifted asset, which is clubbed. Note: The cited NISM Series X-B Investment Adviser Level 2 workbook pages reviewed in the audit support that minor child income may be clubbed with a parent/guardian under Section 64 (with a disability exception), but the higher-income-parent rule and the Rs.1,500 Section 10(32) exemption used to derive Rs.33,500 are not on the pages checked. The figures above reflect the standard Income Tax Act treatment as generally applied in industry practice.
